To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a number of enzymes (including those involved in carbohydrate metabolism) and polysaccharide and lipid stores undergo transient and reversible changes in concentration and/or activity during carcinogenesis induced in liver and pancreas by N-nitrosobis(2-chloroethyl)urea and N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea, in kidney and brain by ethylnitrosourea and in colon by azoxymethane and 1,2-dimethylhydrazine.

the metabolic changes in neoplastic transformation are not a random phenomenon but rather follow a specific pattern, and that the metabolic aberration is a cause and not a consequence of neoplastic transformation.
the hexose-monphosphate shunt, glycolysis, and gluconeogenesis increase during carcinogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the investigation of the biochemical and morphologic changes during the development of neoplastic cells in order to obtain more detailed information on the molecular mechanism(s) underlying the neoplastic transformation.
the elucidation of the role of carbohydrate metabolism in the neoplastic process.
the study of the metabolic changes during neoplastic transformation of cells and the role of these changes in carcinogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the metabolic aberrations observed during neoplastic transformation are not a cause but a consequence of the neoplastic process.
the metabolic changes during carcinogenesis are not only a consequence but also a cause of neoplastic cell proliferation.
the metabolic aberration is a cause rather than a consequence of neoplastic transformation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the changes of the carbohydrate metabolism are not the primary cause of the transformation process, but that the transformation process itself is the cause of the metabolic changes observed in tumor cells.
during carcinogenesis, the neoplastic cells are forced to adapt to the altered conditions by activating alternative pathways.
a disturbance of the carbohydrate metabolism precedes neoplastic cell transformations and that this disturbance may be a cause of carcinogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the modulation of carbohydrate metabolism is not only an important event in carcinogenesis but also a potential target for cancer prevention and therapy.
the changes in carbohydrate metabolism observed during neoplastic transformation are probably not only secondary to an increase in cell proliferation, but may also play a causative role.
the metabolic changes observed during carcinogenesis may be used as markers for the early stages of neoplastic transformation.
